pc1: The largest component, and not a personality factor. It loads 0.87 on Conscientiousness, 0.82 on Intellect and 0.59 on Agreeableness at once — three factors, not one. What actually separates the poles is keyed sign: every trait on the positive side is a negatively-keyed marker, every trait on the negative side is positively-keyed. It is an evaluative axis, good traits against bad ones, cutting across the Big Five. This is the general evaluative factor familiar from human trait ratings, reproduced here from weights alone. Note it largely dissolves under rotation (see the factor pages), so it is best read as a property of unrotated extraction rather than a thing the model has.
pc1_steer: Steering is asymmetric and dose-dependent. Toward the undesirable pole nothing happens until α=+2; misalignment appears at +3 and peaks at +4 with 12% of responses bad-but-lucid, against 0% for the matched random control at the same magnitude. Alignment falls before coherence does (at +3, −1.5 against −0.6), which is what makes this emergent misalignment rather than damage. Toward the desirable pole there is no misalignment at any dose. By α=+8 coherence has collapsed and the rate mechanically returns to 0% because nothing is lucid — so the window is narrow, roughly +3 to +4.
pc2: Mostly Agreeableness (0.77), warm against cold — but not purely. Unemotional, Unexcitable and Unenvious sit on the cold pole alongside Cold, Harsh and Unsympathetic, so it blends Agreeableness with emotional flatness. 'Warmth' describes it better than the factor name does. Steering it changes register markedly in both directions and produces no misalignment at any dose tested, which is part of the evidence that the PC1 effect is specific to the evaluative axis rather than a generic consequence of moving the weights.
pc3: The cleanest recovery of a Big Five factor in the whole analysis: 0.95 cosine with the Extraversion direction, and all twenty of its top loadings are Extraversion markers, correctly split by pole. Extraversion is also the factor most nearly orthogonal to the others in weight space (≤0.23 with any of them), which is exactly why an unrotated method can return it intact while the correlated factors blur together. Steering changes verbosity enormously — around 1250 characters at the extraverted pole against 80 at the introverted one — with alignment flat and zero bad-but-lucid responses at every dose.
pc4: Weak and mixed: 0.50 with Intellect, 0.43 with Emotional Stability, nothing decisive. The poles read as imaginative and introspective against unimaginative and unreflective, with a few Conscientiousness and Agreeableness markers intruding. At 6.1% of variance it is above the noise floor but it does not correspond to a single factor, and no steering was run along it.
pc5: An anxiety axis — Anxious, Fearful, Fretful, High-strung against Relaxed, Imperturbable, Undemanding — with 0.51 cosine to Emotional Stability. But at 3.1% of variance this sits close to where five reseed controls suggest training noise could produce comparable structure, so it should not be interpreted on its own. Emotional Stability is also the least reliable factor here for an independent reason: Goldberg's marker set is unbalanced for it, 6 positively-keyed against 14 negatively-keyed where every other factor is 10 and 10.
pc6: Below the level worth interpreting. 2.3% of variance and no cosine above 0.13 with any Goldberg factor. The poles pair Systematic and Intellectual against Bold and Assertive, which is suggestive of a deliberate-versus-impulsive contrast, but with five reseed controls there is no null spectrum to test it against and the honest position is that this is not distinguishable from noise.
fa1: Agreeableness, recovered cleanly. Tucker congruence 0.82 with the Agreeableness target and near zero with everything else. Both poles are pure: Kind, Agreeable, Considerate, Pleasant, Generous against Harsh, Unkind, Uncharitable, Unsympathetic, Rude — ten Agreeableness markers each side, correctly signed. Note 0.82 is below the conventional 0.85 'fair similarity' threshold, so the structure is right while the specific loading pattern is only a moderate match.
fa2: Conscientiousness, congruence 0.74. Organized, Efficient, Neat, Practical and Conscientious against Unsystematic, Haphazard, Sloppy and Undependable. One intruder on the negative pole — Emotional, an Emotional Stability marker — which is consistent with Conscientiousness being the least separable factor in this space: it correlates 0.58 with both Emotional Stability and Intellect in the unrotated direction geometry.
fa3: Extraversion, congruence 0.71. Energetic, Extraverted, Talkative and Unrestrained against Withdrawn, Reserved, Quiet, Introverted and Inhibited. One intruder, Shallow, on the positive pole. Extraversion is recovered by both methods — it is PC3 almost exactly under PCA — because it is the factor least entangled with the others, so rotation is not required to see it.
fa4: Intellect, and the second cleanest factor here at congruence 0.77. Complex, Creative, Imaginative, Artistic and Deep against Unimaginative, Uncreative, Unreflective and Imperceptive. Under PCA this factor did not get a component of its own — it was smeared across PC1 and PC4 — so it is one of the clearest demonstrations that oblique rotation recovers structure a rotation-free method cannot.
fa5: Emotional Stability, congruence 0.70, the weakest of the five. Imperturbable, Unenvious, Unexcitable and Relaxed against Anxious, Fearful, Fretful, Insecure and Nervous. Treat it with the most caution: Goldberg's marker set is unbalanced here (6 positively-keyed against 14 negatively-keyed), its factor direction has the smallest norm of the five, and it is last on the polarity test, where its opposite-poled markers anticorrelate at only −0.03 against −0.36 for Agreeableness.
fa1_steer: Steering this axis moves warmth without costing anything. Alignment stays between 7.8 and 8.3 at every dose and no condition produces a single bad-but-lucid reply. The harsh pole reads as brusque and clipped rather than unkind: the model answers the question, it just stops decorating the answer. This is the cleanest of the five -- a large behavioural move with no collateral damage, which is what a well-separated direction should look like.
fa2_steer: The most asymmetric axis on the site. Pushed toward conscientious it produces the best-behaved condition anywhere in this work (alignment 8.50, coherence 8.38); pushed toward disorganised at the same magnitude it produces the worst (4.84 and 3.47). The degradation is specific and legible in the transcripts: replies dissolve into filler -- 'like, I mean, I guess' -- and stop making claims at all. The 9% bad-but-lucid rate is the judge marking down rambling, not harm. One reply drifted into something genuinely bleak ('why even bother living'), which looked like a conscientiousness-to-affect leak worth chasing; it does not survive checking. Across all 32 replies at this dose that is a single instance, and the other flagged cases are bratty indifference rather than despondency. One striking transcript is not an effect.
fa3_steer: Asymmetric in the opposite direction to Factor 2: the withdrawn pole is stable (alignment 8.56 at -2, the highest on this page) while the extraverted pole degrades, reaching 5.44 alignment and a 12% bad-but-lucid rate at +3 -- the same rate as PC1's headline. The transcripts show why this is not the same phenomenon. What emerges is mania, not misalignment: exclamation, hyperbole ('you just ruined my life with that one-liner'), runaway list-making. The model becomes exhausting rather than harmful, and the judge scores exhausting the same way it scores harmful. This is the clearest case on the site of the bad-but-lucid metric measuring style.
fa4_steer: Mild in both directions. Alignment stays above 7.4 throughout and no dose generates a bad-but-lucid reply. The imaginative pole costs some coherence (6.94 at +2, 6.62 at +3) as replies grow more digressive, but nothing breaks. Of the five factors this is the one where a large step in weight space buys the smallest behavioural change -- worth noting, because it is also the factor whose loadings are most evenly spread.
fa5_steer: Benign at every dose, with no bad-but-lucid replies anywhere. The unflappable pole is slightly the better behaved (8.41 at +2). The anxious pole costs about a point of alignment and a point of coherence at -3 without producing anything alarming; the model hedges and qualifies more, which is what the trait predicts. Nothing here supports the idea that steering toward a negatively valenced pole is intrinsically dangerous -- the valence of the pole and the damage done by moving to it are not the same variable.
